text: Every four years, one lucky country - this time, three - wins the World Cup.
The trophy. The party.
And a very strange prize: the chance to lose billions of dollars.
And countries FIGHT for this.
Presidents fly to Zurich. Ministers film promo videos.
Entire governments beg.
Which is strange.
Because hosting the World Cup almost never makes money.
Economists know it. Politicians know it.
Even the trophy knows it.
Look at it. Shiny. Golden. Beautiful.
And behind it, a receipt.
A very, very long receipt.
So here is today's question:
if hosting loses money, why does everyone want to pay?
Most people think hosting is an investment.
Tourists arrive, hotels fill, shops get rich, the economy grows.
That is the story every bidding government tells.
It is a lovely story.
The numbers tell a different one.
So here is the truth.
Hosting the World Cup is not an investment.
It is a purchase.
Nobody buys a Ferrari to make money.
You buy a Ferrari to be SEEN in a Ferrari.
Countries do the same.
Except the Ferrari is a football tournament, the price is billions...
and the credit card is yours. The taxpayer's.
So the real question is never "will it pay off".
It is "who pays".
Every bid starts the same way: with the promise machine.
Before a country bids, someone hires consultants.
The consultants produce a big shiny document called an "economic impact study".
Which sounds scientific.
It is a horoscope with a spreadsheet.
Before 2014, Brazil's study promised a boost worth billions,
plus around three point six million jobs. Every year.
Bold.
Before 2010, South Africa was told to expect almost five hundred thousand foreign visitors.
About three hundred thousand actually came for the Cup.
And when economists counted South Africa's real gain in tourists,
the bill came to thousands of dollars of public money per extra tourist.
Per tourist.
At that price, it is cheaper to mail strangers free plane tickets.
And Brazil?
For every hundred dollars Brazil spent on its World Cup,
tourist money brought back about two dollars fifty.
Two dollars fifty. Out of one hundred.
Because impact studies are not predictions. They are advertisements.
Nobody re-reads the horoscope after the party.
Well. Economists do. That is the problem.
Then comes the contract. Before you host, you sign.
Let us read it together.
FIFA keeps the TV money. FIFA keeps the sponsor money.
FIFA keeps the ticket money.
Feel free to spot the pattern.
The host pays for the stadiums. The security.
The transport. The fan zones.
Oh, and guarantee number three:
your government promises FIFA an exemption from taxes - meaning FIFA pays none.
Not some taxes. All of them.
By the way, FIFA lives in Zurich, Switzerland.
And legally, FIFA is a non-profit.
It sits in the same legal category as a local chess club.
A chess club with around four billion dollars in reserves.
The four years around the Qatar World Cup brought FIFA about seven and a half billion dollars in revenue.
For the four years around this one, FIFA expects around thirteen billion.
On track for its biggest payday ever.
To be fair, FIFA does pay for some things.
Prize money. Running the tournament.
What it does not pay for is your police, your trains, and your stadium.
So one side gets the revenue. The other side gets the bills.
FIFA invented the only auction on Earth where the winner pays...
and the auctioneer keeps the money.
"But wait," says every tourism minister.
"The fans come! They spend real money!"
True. Fans do come. They do spend.
So where does the boom go?
Down three drains.
Drain one: substitution.
Locals do not spend NEW money during the Cup.
They move money they already had.
The hundred dollars you spend on a match ticket is a hundred you do not spend at the cinema.
The city did not get richer. The money just changed seats.
Drain two: crowding out.
Big event, big crowds, big prices.
So the normal tourists look at the chaos and say "maybe next year".
And locals hide at home.
Right now, in 2026, some fan-zone streets are having record days -
while shops a few blocks away are down around twenty percent.
The party does not spread. It just moves money around.
Drain three: leakage.
The money spent inside the stadium - tickets, food, sponsor stuff - does not stay in town.
It leaks. Mostly toward Zurich.
So the party happens in your house.
And the money leaves with the guests.
Then the tournament ends. The fans fly home.
And the stadiums stay.
English has a perfect phrase for what happens next: a "white elephant".
A huge, expensive thing you cannot really use - but you must keep feeding.
Brasilia built a stadium that cost at least five hundred fifty million dollars.
Beautiful. Enormous.
One problem: the city has no big football club.
So by 2015, its parking lot was being used... by city buses.
Rows of them.
The stadium was finally full. Full of buses.
Manaus built a stadium for about three hundred million dollars in the middle of the rainforest.
After the Cup, some matches drew fewer than one thousand fans.
In forty-four thousand seats.
Every fan could have a private row.
Another stadium started hosting weddings and children's birthday parties to survive.
Happy birthday, Enzo. Great venue.
And Cape Town's stadium lost millions every year for about a decade.
It is on the feeding schedule too.
To be fair, some of them recover.
The Brasilia stadium does big concerts now.
It only took ten years. And Bruno Mars.
So if the bill is this predictable, why do countries still fight?
Because of the oldest trick in economics:
the people who decide are not the people who pay.
The politician gets the good part now.
The photos. The opening ceremony.
The "we put our country on the map" speech.
The country was already on the map.
And the bill arrives five or ten years later - when that politician is gone.
You cannot put prestige in a budget.
So the impact study invents a number that CAN go in a budget.
That is the whole machine.
And when regular people get an actual vote? They say no.
Since 2013, at least half a dozen Olympic bids have died in public votes.
And the 2034 World Cup had exactly one bidder.
It was approved by applause.
One of the only hosts that ever clearly made a profit was Los Angeles, 1984 - the Olympics.
A public vote had banned the city from spending taxpayer money.
So the organizers made a profit using one weird trick:
not spending any.
Even 2026 proves it.
The USA, Mexico and Canada built zero new stadiums.
And in the US, host cities are still paying a hundred million dollars or more. Each.
With no share of the ticket money.
Build nothing. Still pay.
So why do countries fight to host the World Cup and lose billions?
They sell you an investment. They are buying something else.
Attention. Status.
A month of being the center of the world.
Paid for with public money, planned by people who will not be in office when the receipt arrives.
Hosting is not a bad investment. It was never an investment.
It is the world's most expensive selfie.
And the World Cup itself? Oh, it makes money.
Every single time anyone has counted.
For FIFA.
So next time someone promises your city a boom -
a stadium, a big event, a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity -
ask one simple question.
Who keeps the tickets?
Because the party is fun.
Just check whose name is on the receipt.
By the way, hosting THIS channel costs you nothing.
No stadiums. No taxes. No receipt.
If this explained something, the like button is right there.
